_comment: Every mechanism on the page. Sorted at render time by `date`, which is always the first PUBLIC appearance - arXiv v1 submission date, or a dated release/post where the idea genuinely arrived that way. `dateKind` says which. Nothing here is dated from memory; see README.md for how each was checked.

eras.name: Buy exactness, worry about the bill later
eras.beat: Attention wins by being exact and parallel: every token sees every other token in one step, and nothing has to be unrolled. The quadratic cost is known from day one and is simply not the binding constraint yet, because nobody is running 100k-token contexts. The only thing being fixed in this era is that attention is order-blind, so position has to be bolted on somehow.

eras.name: The efficiency zoo attacks the wrong bottleneck
eras.beat: Eighteen months, six major papers, one target: the O(n²) term. Sparsity, hashing, low-rank projection, kernel tricks - every angle gets tried. Almost none of it ships. In the same window a quieter paper (MQA) attacks the KV cache instead and is ignored for three and a half years, because in 2019 the field is training models, not serving them.

eras.name: Position gets rethought, and a kernel beats the zoo
eras.beat: RoPE and ALiBi replace additive position embeddings with things that degrade gracefully rather than falling off a cliff. Then FlashAttention arrives and quietly wins the efficiency argument by refusing to approximate at all - it changes no mathematics and returns a bit-exact result, it just stops writing the score matrix to memory. Half the zoo was solving a memory problem while believing it was a compute problem.

eras.name: Serving becomes the constraint, and length becomes the product
eras.beat: Open weights plus deployment economics change what counts as a good idea. Five separate attacks on the KV cache land inside twelve months after four years of near-silence. Simultaneously, context length becomes a marketing number, so a whole family appears whose only job is to map positions the model has never seen onto ones it has - two of the most consequential of which were a blog post and a Reddit thread.

eras.name: Sparsity becomes trainable, and memory gets rebuilt on purpose
eras.beat: The two threads converge. Sparsity finally ships - but only once the selection is learned end-to-end rather than hand-designed. And linear attention comes back not as a cheap approximation of attention but as a deliberately engineered recurrent memory with a gate and an edit rule. Nobody, however, gives up exact attention entirely: the 2025 architectures are hybrids, and that reluctance is the most informative fact on the page.

mechanisms.name: Learned absolute position embeddings
mechanisms.problem: Attention is a set operation - permute the tokens and the maths is completely unchanged. Something has to tell the model that word 3 came before word 9, and the first answer was the most obvious one available: learn a vector for each slot.
how: Keep a trainable table of nmax × d vectors, one per absolute position, and add the row for position i to the token embedding at position i before the first layer. Position is then just another feature the network can read.

It is the cheapest possible fix and it works well, which is why it survived into BERT, GPT-1, GPT-2 and GPT-3 despite the original Transformer preferring sinusoids. Gehring et al. used it in a convolutional sequence model a month before the Transformer paper appeared.
mechanisms.math: xᵢ = TokenEmb(tᵢ) + PosEmb[i]
pros: Trivial to implement, and completely free at inference - a table lookup and an addition.
Maximally expressive: the model can learn whatever quirk of position the data actually contains, with no prior imposed on it.
Empirically it matches sinusoidal encodings within the trained range, which is what let it dominate the entire BERT/GPT era.
cons: It cannot extrapolate at all. Position 2049 in a model trained to 2048 has no row in the table. Not a degradation - an absent parameter.
Positions seen rarely in training get badly-fit embeddings, so quality is uneven across the context even inside the trained range.
It encodes absolute position, but almost every linguistic relationship you care about is relative. The model has to spend capacity subtracting one position from another itself.
Adds parameters that scale with the context you want, which becomes absurd once contexts reach 128k.
mechanisms.pick: You are training an encoder or a short-context model with a fixed, known maximum length and you want the simplest thing that could possibly work. For classification-style workloads under 512 tokens it is still perfectly defensible.
mechanisms.avoid: Anything where you may later want to extend context, or any decoder aiming past its training length - you will have to retrofit RoPE or ALiBi, and that is a retraining-scale change.
mechanisms.shipped: ConvS2S, BERT, GPT-1, GPT-2, GPT-3, OPT, ViT

citation.title: Convolutional Sequence to Sequence Learning
citation.authors: Jonas Gehring, Michael Auli, David Grangier, Denis Yarats, Yann N. Dauphin (Facebook AI Research)
citation.note: Position embeddings as a learned table predate this in other architectures, but this is the first-appearance date used here because it is the paper the Transformer authors themselves cite for the learned-embedding variant they compared against. BERT (arXiv:1810.04805, 11 Oct 2018) is what made it the default.

mechanisms.name: Scaled dot-product attention (the standard one)
mechanisms.problem: Recurrence forced sequential computation - to know the state at step 1000 you had to compute steps 1 to 999 first - which made training slow and long-range gradients weak. The problem was: can a sequence model relate any two positions in one step, and train on all positions in parallel?
how: Every token emits three vectors: a query (what am I looking for), a key (what am I), and a value (what I hand over if picked). Score each query against every key with a dot product, divide by √dk so the logits stay in a range softmax can handle, softmax each row into a distribution, and return that weighted average of the values.

This is content-addressed lookup, done softly and differentiably. Path length between any two tokens is one, regardless of distance - which is the entire reason it beat LSTMs on long-range dependencies.

Multi-head runs h of these in parallel on d/h-dimensional slices and concatenates, so different heads can specialise (one tracks syntax, one tracks coreference, one just attends to the previous token).

The √dk is not cosmetic: dot products of two random d-dimensional vectors have variance proportional to d, so without it softmax saturates and gradients vanish at exactly the scale you want to train at.
mechanisms.math: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q Kᵀ / √dₖ ) V
pros: Exact. Every token genuinely sees every other token; nothing is approximated, dropped or summarised. Every mechanism after this one is measured against it and every one loses something.
Fully parallel over sequence positions during training - no recurrence to unroll, which is what made scaling laws affordable in the first place.
Constant path length between any two positions, so gradients do not have to survive 1000 sequential steps.
It is a general associative-memory primitive, not a language trick, which is why the same block works for images, audio, protein structure and video.
cons: Quadratic compute and quadratic activation memory. Double the context, quadruple the work. This is the bill the whole rest of the page is arguing about.

The KV cache grows without bound and must be re-read in full for every generated token, which makes decoding memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. At long context this hurts more than the quadratic term.
Completely order-blind on its own - it needs a positional scheme bolted on, and that bolt-on became a research area of its own.

Softmax forces every row to sum to 1, so a token with genuinely nothing to attend to must still put its probability mass somewhere. That single fact causes attention sinks, massive activations and several quantisation headaches downstream.
mechanisms.pick: Almost always, at short-to-moderate context, and always as the reference you compare against. If your context fits comfortably in memory and you have FlashAttention, dense attention is fast, exact, well-understood and has no failure modes anyone will surprise you with.
mechanisms.avoid: Contexts in the hundreds of thousands, high-concurrency serving where the KV cache dominates your GPU memory, or edge deployment - not because it is wrong, but because you are paying for exactness you may not need on every layer.
mechanisms.shipped: Everything. BERT, the entire GPT line, T5, ViT, Whisper, and as the fallback path inside every hybrid model on this page.

citation.title: Attention Is All You Need
citation.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin (Google Brain / Google Research / U. Toronto)
citation.note: Attention itself is older - Bahdanau et al. (arXiv:1409.0473, 1 Sep 2014) introduced additive attention for NMT, and Luong et al. (arXiv:1508.04025, 17 Aug 2015) introduced the multiplicative form. What this paper contributes is removing the recurrence entirely and adding the √d scaling and multi-head split. The timeline dates the mechanism as we use it, so it sits here.

mechanisms.name: Sinusoidal position encoding
mechanisms.problem: A learned position table has a hard ceiling and burns parameters. Could position instead be a fixed function - defined for every integer, so that nothing structurally prevents the model from being fed a position it never saw in training?
how: Give each embedding dimension a sine (or cosine) of position at a different wavelength, geometrically spaced from about 2π up to about 10000·2π. Low dimensions oscillate fast and encode fine local offsets; high dimensions oscillate slowly and encode roughly where in the document you are.

The elegant property the paper advertises: for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos) - a rotation. So relative offsets are in principle linearly recoverable, which is the seed of the idea RoPE later makes explicit and exact.
Zero parameters, computed once into a lookup table, added to the token embedding exactly like the learned version.
mechanisms.math: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)),  PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d))
pros: No parameters at all, and defined for arbitrarily large positions - the values never run out.
Encodes relative offset as a linear map, which gives the model a genuinely useful structure to exploit rather than an arbitrary table.
Deterministic and reproducible; no risk of an under-trained embedding at a rarely-seen position.
cons: The extrapolation promise mostly does not cash out. The values are well-defined past the training length, but the model has never seen that combination of phases, and quality degrades badly anyway. This is the single most common misconception about sinusoidal encoding.
Adding position to the token embedding means position and content compete for the same vector space, and the position signal gets diluted layer by layer.
Still absolute, so relative distance has to be reconstructed by the model.
In head-to-head tests it is roughly a wash with the learned table inside the training range - so it bought elegance, not accuracy.
mechanisms.pick: Fixed-length encoders and any setting where you want zero positional parameters and a well-understood baseline. It remains a reasonable default for non-text modalities where the sequence length is known.
mechanisms.avoid: Long-context decoders. If you need length generalisation, RoPE with a scaling scheme or ALiBi will beat it, and the belief that sinusoids extrapolate for free has burned a lot of people.
mechanisms.shipped: Original Transformer, Whisper (encoder), many diffusion and vision models for timestep and patch position

citation.title: Attention Is All You Need (§3.5, Positional Encoding)
citation.authors: Ashish Vaswani et al. (Google Brain / Google Research)
citation.note: Same paper and therefore the same date as standard attention - it is §3.5 of it. Listed separately because it is a separable mechanism with its own trade-offs and its own successors.

mechanisms.name: Relative position representations
mechanisms.problem: Absolute position answers "where am I in the document", but essentially every syntactic relationship you care about is about distance: the adjective before the noun, the verb three words back. Encoding absolute position and making the model subtract was wasteful and did not generalise across shifts.
how: Drop position from the input embedding. Instead, add a learned vector that depends on the relative offset i - j directly inside the attention computation, in the key term (and optionally the value term).
Clip the offset at some maximum k, so distances beyond k all share one embedding. This bounds the number of parameters and lets any distance be represented, if coarsely.
mechanisms.math: eᵢⱼ = qᵢ · (kⱼ + aᵢⱼᴷ)ᵀ / √dₖ,   aᵢⱼᴷ = wᴷ[clip(j - i, k)]
pros: Translation-invariant: the same phrase gets the same treatment at position 10 and position 1000, which is what you actually want linguistically.
Measurably better than absolute encodings on translation quality in the original paper, and it opened the whole relative-position line that leads to RoPE and ALiBi.
Handles sequences longer than training more gracefully than an absolute table, because clipped far distances at least have a defined embedding.
cons: Slow. The naive implementation needs a separate relative-embedding tensor per query position, which is materially more compute and memory than an additive absolute encoding - this is why it did not immediately take over.
The clipping means all distances beyond k are literally indistinguishable to the model.
It interferes with KV-cache reuse and with efficient fused kernels, because the bias term is not a simple function of the cached keys.
Adds parameters and a hyperparameter (k) that nobody has a principled way to choose.
mechanisms.pick: Mostly of historical importance now - but if you are training an encoder from scratch at moderate length and want relative semantics without RoPE's rotation machinery, it is simple and it works.
mechanisms.avoid: Any long-context decoder, or anything that needs FlashAttention-class kernels - RoPE gives you relative semantics with none of the memory cost and composes cleanly with fused kernels.
mechanisms.shipped: Transformer-XL (a reparameterised variant), Music Transformer, Wav2Vec 2.0

citation.title: Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations
citation.authors: Peter Shaw, Jakob Uszkoreit, Ashish Vaswani (Google Brain)

mechanisms.name: Segment recurrence + relative encoding (Transformer-XL)
mechanisms.problem: Long documents were being chopped into fixed segments that could not see each other at all - a phenomenon the authors named context fragmentation. The model would hit a hard wall at the segment boundary and lose everything before it, mid-sentence.
how: Cache the hidden states of the previous segment and let the current segment attend to them, with the gradient stopped at the boundary. You get a receding-window memory that costs no extra attention compute at training time.

This breaks absolute position encoding outright - position 0 of segment 2 and position 0 of segment 1 would collide - so the paper introduces a reparameterised relative encoding with sinusoidal relative terms plus learned global content and position biases.

costs.compute: O(n²) per segment, not per document

pros: First mechanism to give a decoder a context genuinely longer than its attention window, and it did so at essentially no extra attention cost.
Much faster evaluation - no need to re-encode a full window for every new token, which the paper measured at up to 1800×.
Its relative-position formulation is cleaner than Shaw's and directly influenced everything after it.
cons: The memory is read-only and not trained through - gradients stop at the segment boundary, so the model never learns how to write a good memory, only how to read a stale one.
Information decays as it passes through segments; this is a soft, uncontrolled forgetting, not a designed one.
The relative encoding costs extra compute and complicates fused-kernel implementations.
Superseded in practice: RoPE plus a long training context does the same job without the recurrence bookkeeping.
mechanisms.pick: Largely historical, but the pattern - cache the previous chunk's states and attend to them - is exactly what modern chunked-prefill and streaming implementations do, so it is worth understanding.
mechanisms.avoid: New work. Use RoPE with a scaling method, or a hybrid linear/attention stack, both of which handle length better and train end-to-end.
mechanisms.shipped: Transformer-XL, XLNet, Compressive Transformer

citation.title: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
citation.authors: Zihang Dai, Zhilin Yang, Yiming Yang, Jaime Carbonell, Quoc V. Le, Ruslan Salakhutdinov (CMU / Google Brain)

mechanisms.name: Fixed sparse attention patterns
mechanisms.problem: OpenAI wanted to model images, audio and long text as raw sequences of tens of thousands of elements. At n = 12288 the score matrix alone is 150M entries per head per layer. The quadratic term stopped being a theoretical concern and became the thing standing in the way.
how: Factorise the dense attention pattern into two cheap ones applied in different heads or layers: a local pattern covering the last √n positions, and a strided pattern covering every √n-th position. Any two tokens are then connected in at most two hops instead of one.
Total cost drops to O(n√n). The paper pairs this with a memory-efficient recomputation scheme, and this is also where the widely-copied residual/init scaling for very deep Transformers comes from.
pros: First credible demonstration that you can drop most of the attention matrix and still model hard data - it set density records on Enwik8, CIFAR-10 and raw audio.
Simple, predictable, and the pattern is static, so kernels can be written for it and the cost is known up front.
Directly enabled a generation of long-sequence generative models, including the original DALL-E and Jukebox.
cons: The pattern is a human guess about what matters, fixed before the model sees any data. If the important token is not on the stride, it is unreachable in one hop and the model has to route around it.
Two-hop routing burns representational capacity on relaying information that dense attention would have moved directly.
Needs custom kernels to realise the theoretical saving; a naive implementation is no faster.
The √n factorisation is tuned to the sequence length, so it does not adapt as context grows.
mechanisms.pick: When you genuinely have a fixed, known, very long sequence with strong locality - raw audio, high-resolution images - and you can afford a custom kernel. As a general LLM mechanism it has been superseded by trainable selection.
mechanisms.avoid: General language modelling in 2025. The 2025 sparse methods do the same thing with a learned gate and beat this comfortably; a fixed pattern is now the worst of both worlds.
mechanisms.shipped: Sparse Transformer, DALL-E 1, Jukebox, GPT-3 (alternating dense and locally-banded sparse layers)

citation.title: Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers
citation.authors: Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Ilya Sutskever (OpenAI)

mechanisms.name: Relative position bias buckets (T5)
mechanisms.problem: Shaw's relative embeddings were expensive - a whole vector per relative offset, added inside the attention computation. How much of that is actually load-bearing?
how: Almost none of it, as it turns out. Reduce the entire relative-position signal to a single learned scalar per head, added to the attention logit, and share it across all layers.

Bucket the relative distances logarithmically - exact buckets for small offsets, increasingly coarse ones as distance grows, all distances past a cutoff sharing one bucket. Nearby matters precisely, far matters vaguely.
mechanisms.math: eᵢⱼ = qᵢ kⱼᵀ / √dₖ + b_head[bucket(i - j)]
pros: Almost free in parameters and compute, and it matched much more elaborate schemes - a genuinely useful negative result about how much positional machinery you need.
Log-bucketing is a good prior: local distinctions matter, distant ones do not need resolution.
Because the bias is a scalar added to the logit, it composes with anything, including fused kernels.
Degrades gracefully rather than breaking past training length - all far distances just land in the last bucket.
cons: Beyond the last bucket the model is genuinely blind to distance - 5,000 tokens back and 50,000 tokens back are identical to it.
A single scalar per head cannot express direction-and-content-dependent positional effects that a full embedding can.
Sharing the bias across layers saves parameters but removes the possibility of layers specialising by range.
Encoder-decoder-shaped: the bucketing scheme was tuned for T5's workloads and is not obviously right for 100k-token decoders.
mechanisms.pick: Encoder-decoder models, and anywhere you want relative position for near-zero cost. Still the default in T5-derived architectures and in a lot of non-text Transformers.
mechanisms.avoid: Long-context decoders where distinguishing 10k from 100k tokens back actually matters - the buckets saturate and you lose the distinction entirely.
mechanisms.shipped: T5, mT5, Flan-T5, UL2, and (with modifications) many vision Transformers

citation.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
citation.authors: Colin Raffel, Noam Shazeer, Adam Roberts, Katherine Lee, Sharan Narang, Michael Matena, Yanqi Zhou, Wei Li, Peter J. Liu (Google)
citation.note: The relative-bias scheme is §2.1 of the T5 paper rather than its headline contribution, but this is its first public appearance and it is dated accordingly.

mechanisms.name: Multi-query attention (MQA)
mechanisms.problem: Shazeer noticed that incremental decoding was not compute-bound at all. Generating one token requires re-reading the entire KV cache from memory, and the cache is proportional to layers × heads × context. The arithmetic intensity of decoding is terrible, and the bottleneck is bandwidth, not FLOPs.
how: Keep all h query heads, but give the whole layer one single key head and one single value head, shared by every query head. The KV cache shrinks by a factor of h - typically 32× or 64×.
Nothing else changes. Queries still project per-head, the scores are still per-head, and only the thing you have to store and re-read is collapsed.
mechanisms.math: KV cache: 2·L·H·d_h  →  2·L·1·d_h  per token
pros: An order-of-magnitude cut in the thing that actually limits serving. Larger batches, longer contexts, and much faster decoding on the same hardware.
Changes nothing about the mathematics of attention, so it composes with every other mechanism here.
Training compute is barely affected - during training you are compute-bound anyway, so this is nearly free upside.
cons: Measurable quality degradation. All query heads must agree on one representation of the past; heads can no longer specialise in what they retrieve, only in what they ask for.
Reported to be less stable to train and more prone to quality cliffs than MHA - part of why GQA exists.
Converting an existing MHA checkpoint is not free; you have to uptrain, and naive conversion loses a lot.
Saves nothing during prefill of a long prompt, where you are compute-bound - it only helps the decode phase.
mechanisms.pick: Very high-throughput serving of a smaller model where memory is the binding constraint and you can absorb a small quality cost - or on-device, where memory is not negotiable.
mechanisms.avoid: Frontier-quality models. GQA gets you most of the memory saving for a fraction of the quality loss, and there is essentially no reason to choose pure MQA over GQA today.
mechanisms.shipped: PaLM, Falcon, StarCoder, Gemini (reported)

citation.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need
citation.authors: Noam Shazeer (Google)
citation.note: One of the clearest timing stories on this page: published November 2019, essentially ignored for three and a half years, then suddenly essential once the industry moved from training models to serving them. The mechanism did not change. The economics did.

mechanisms.name: Top-k / explicit sparse attention
mechanisms.problem: Fixed sparse patterns guess where the useful tokens are before looking. But softmax attention already computes a relevance score for every pair - and empirically the distribution is extremely concentrated, with most of the mass on a handful of tokens. Why not just keep those?
how: Compute the scores as normal, then for each query keep only the k largest logits and set the rest to -∞ before the softmax. The surviving distribution is renormalised over k entries.

The mask is now input-dependent: a different set of tokens survives for every query and every input. That is the key difference from every fixed pattern before it - the model, not the designer, chooses.
The paper's argument is not primarily speed but quality: forcing concentration removes noise from irrelevant tokens and sharpens the attended context.
pros: The selection is data-dependent, so nothing important is structurally unreachable the way it is with a fixed stride.
Improves quality in the original paper, not just speed - concentration acts as a denoiser on the attention distribution.
Conceptually simple, and it is the direct ancestor of every learned-selection method that ships in 2025.
cons: You still have to compute all n² scores to know which k to keep, so the naive version saves no attention FLOPs at all. This is the central problem, and it is why practical versions must select at block granularity rather than per token.
Top-k is a sort - branchy, irregular, and hostile to the dense matrix pipelines GPUs are built for. Wall-clock speedups are much harder to get than the FLOP count suggests.
Hard selection is not differentiable through the discarded entries, so gradients only flow to the winners and the selection cannot easily be learned.
k is a fixed budget, but the true number of relevant tokens varies enormously by query - one size does not fit all rows.
mechanisms.pick: As a component, not a system: modern block-sparse methods are top-k on blocks with a cheap proxy score. As a standalone at inference, when you want the quality benefit of concentration and are not chasing speed.
mechanisms.avoid: Anywhere you expect the FLOP saving to become a wall-clock saving without careful kernel work. Naive top-k attention is usually slower than dense attention with FlashAttention.
mechanisms.shipped: Rarely alone; the idea reappears as the selection branch of NSA, MoBA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention

citation.title: Explicit Sparse Transformer: Concentrated Attention Through Explicit Selection
citation.authors: Guangxiang Zhao, Junyang Lin, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xuancheng Ren, Qi Su, Xu Sun (Peking University / Alibaba)

mechanisms.name: LSH attention (Reformer)
mechanisms.problem: If softmax attention is dominated by the few largest dot products, then the real task is nearest-neighbour search in query-key space - and computing all n² products to find the nearest neighbours is a spectacularly inefficient way to do nearest-neighbour search.
how: Hash queries and keys with a random-projection LSH scheme so that vectors with large dot products land in the same bucket with high probability. Sort by bucket, chunk, and attend only within a chunk and its neighbour.
Tie queries and keys to the same projection so a query and its own key always collide. Run several independent hash rounds to reduce the chance of missing a true neighbour.
Combine with reversible residual layers so activations do not have to be stored for the backward pass - the paper's memory claim depends on both tricks together.
pros: Genuinely sub-quadratic with a principled justification, rather than a hand-drawn pattern - it targets exactly the entries softmax would have kept.
Reversible layers cut activation memory dramatically and are a reusable idea in their own right.
Demonstrated 64k-token sequences on a single accelerator in 2020, which was startling at the time.
cons: The approximation is stochastic - a genuinely relevant key can simply fail to collide, and you will never know. Quality depends on the number of hash rounds, which eats the speedup.
Hashing, sorting and chunking add large constant factors, so it only wins at very long sequences; below roughly 2k tokens it is slower than dense attention.
Complex to implement and to debug; the reversible-layer machinery interacts awkwardly with mixed precision.
Ties queries and keys to a shared projection, which is a real restriction on what attention can express.
mechanisms.pick: Very long single sequences where an approximate nearest-neighbour view is acceptable and you cannot afford dense attention at all. In practice this is now a narrow niche.
mechanisms.avoid: Anything under about 4k tokens, and any production decoder - FlashAttention made exact attention fast enough that a stochastic approximation is a hard sell.
mechanisms.shipped: Reformer; the LSH-attention idea persists in retrieval-augmented and memory-augmented designs

citation.title: Reformer: The Efficient Transformer
citation.authors: Nikita Kitaev, Łukasz Kaiser, Anselm Levskaya (UC Berkeley / Google Research)

mechanisms.name: Sliding window attention
mechanisms.problem: Most of what a token needs is nearby. Paying to compare token 40,000 against token 3 - for every single pair - to discover that they are unrelated is the most obviously wasteful thing dense attention does on long documents.
how: Restrict each query to the previous W tokens. Compute per token becomes constant rather than linear in context, total compute becomes O(n·W), and at inference the KV cache stops growing once it reaches W.
Information still travels further than W, but it does so through depth: stacking L layers of window W gives an effective receptive field of roughly L·W, exactly like a stack of convolutions.

Longformer adds two things to the plain band: dilated windows in upper layers to widen the field for free, and a few global tokens (such as [CLS] or the question in a QA pair) that attend everywhere and are attended by everyone.
mechanisms.math: attend(i) = { j : i - W < j ≤ i },  cost O(n·W),  cache capped at W
pros: Linear compute and a bounded KV cache - the only mechanism in the 2020 zoo that fixes both of attention's costs at once, which is why it is the one that actually shipped.
Dead simple, needs no special kernel to be correct, and has an exact, predictable cost you can budget for.
Matches locality in real data: for most tokens, nearly all the attention mass genuinely is nearby.
Composes cleanly with everything - you can interleave window layers with full-attention layers and tune the ratio, which is exactly what 2024-2025 models do.
cons: Long-range recall is destroyed at a single layer and only partly reconstructed through depth. Information relayed layer by layer is lossy - this is emphatically not the same as attending directly.
Exact retrieval past the window is unreliable, which is precisely what long-context benchmarks test. A needle at position 5,000 with W=4,096 may be genuinely unreachable.
W is a hard architectural commitment: too small and the model is myopic, too large and you have not saved anything.
Naive implementations at generation time can silently evict the earliest tokens and destroy fluency entirely - which is the specific failure that attention sinks were invented to fix.
mechanisms.pick: Long documents with strong locality, streaming or always-on workloads where the cache must not grow, and as the cheap layer type in a hybrid stack. If your task is summarisation or classification rather than exact retrieval, this is often all you need.
mechanisms.avoid: Needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, long-horizon agent traces, or anything where a fact from 100k tokens ago must be recalled verbatim. Use it interleaved with full attention instead of alone.
mechanisms.shipped: Longformer, BigBird, Mistral 7B, Mixtral, Gemma 2 and 3 (alternating local/global), Llama 4, GPT-OSS, Command R

citation.title: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
citation.authors: Iz Beltagy, Matthew E. Peters, Arman Cohan (Allen Institute for AI)
citation.note: Local/banded attention is older than this paper - it appears in the Sparse Transformer (Apr 2019) and in image Transformers before that. Longformer is dated here because it is the paper that defined the sliding-window-plus-global recipe as a reusable mechanism, and it is the direct ancestor of the sliding windows shipping in production decoders today. The moment it became a production default is separately datable: Mistral 7B was announced on the Mistral AI blog on 27 September 2023 (arXiv:2310.06825 followed on 10 October), and shipped a 4096-token sliding window in a model people actually deployed.

mechanisms.name: Low-rank projected attention (Linformer)
mechanisms.problem: An empirical observation with real teeth: the attention matrix, measured on trained models, is approximately low-rank. Its spectrum decays fast. So why store and compute an n×n object at all?
how: Project the keys and values down the sequence dimension - not the feature dimension - with learned matrices, from length n to a fixed k (typically 256). Attention then runs between n queries and k projected keys.
Cost becomes O(n·k), which is linear in n for fixed k. The paper backs the construction with a Johnson-Lindenstrauss argument.
pros: Genuinely linear, very simple to implement, and it needs no custom kernel - it is two extra matrix multiplies.
The low-rank claim is an empirical measurement rather than an assumption, and it holds up well for encoder workloads.
Strong results on long-document classification at a fraction of the cost.
cons: It cannot do causal masking properly. The projection mixes across all positions including future ones, so it is fundamentally an encoder mechanism. That alone excluded it from the entire generative-LLM era.
The projection matrices are tied to a fixed sequence length n, so the model does not transfer to other lengths without surgery.
Compressing to k vectors is a hard information bottleneck - exact retrieval of a specific rare token is not recoverable from a 256-vector summary.
The low-rank property is a property of trained attention matrices on certain data; it is not guaranteed, and it fails exactly on the retrieval-heavy inputs you most care about.
mechanisms.pick: Long-document encoder tasks - classification, retrieval scoring, embedding models - where there is no causal constraint and the sequence length is fixed and known.
mechanisms.avoid: Any autoregressive decoder. This is not a tuning problem, it is structural.
mechanisms.shipped: Rare in production; the idea survives in linear-attention and compressed-KV designs

citation.title: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
citation.authors: Sinong Wang, Belinda Z. Li, Madian Khabsa, Han Fang, Hao Ma (Facebook AI)

mechanisms.name: Linear attention (kernel feature maps)
mechanisms.problem: The quadratic cost comes from one specific place: softmax(QKᵀ) forces you to build the n×n matrix before you can multiply by V. If the similarity function were a plain inner product of feature maps, you could reassociate the multiplication and never build it at all.
how: Replace exp(q·k) with φ(q)·φ(k)ᵀ for some non-negative feature map φ (the paper uses elu(x)+1). Then by associativity compute φ(K)ᵀV first - a d×d matrix, independent of sequence length - and multiply the queries into it.
Cost becomes O(n·d²): linear in sequence length. Memory becomes constant.

The observation that gives the paper its title: in the causal case this is exactly a recurrent network. The running sum St = St-1 + φ(kt)vtᵀ is a fixed-size hidden state, so autoregressive generation is O(1) per token with no KV cache at all. Attention, minus the softmax, is an RNN.
mechanisms.math: φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV) instead of (φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ)V   —   Sₜ = Sₜ₋₁ + φ(kₜ)vₜᵀ

costs.state: fixed d × d, no KV cache

pros: Linear in time and constant in memory, and unlike Linformer it works causally. Generation needs no growing cache whatsoever.
Reported ~4000× faster autoregressive generation than a vanilla Transformer at long context in the original paper.
The RNN equivalence is one of the most important conceptual results on this page - it is what makes the entire 2024-2025 recurrent-memory revival possible.
Train in parallel (as attention), serve as a recurrence. You get both modes from one set of weights.
cons: Materially worse quality than softmax attention on retrieval-style tasks, and the reason is structural: the whole past is squashed into a fixed d×d state, so exact recall of an arbitrary earlier token is simply not available.
Softmax is doing real work - it sharpens the distribution. A plain inner product spreads attention out, and the model loses the ability to focus hard on one token.

The state is written to by addition only. Every new key-value pair is added forever, so the state saturates and old information smears rather than being replaced. This is the specific defect that the delta rule fixes.
Numerically finicky: the normaliser can approach zero and the choice of feature map matters far more than it should.
mechanisms.pick: Very long sequences where constant memory is the whole game, streaming inference, or on-device deployment - and today, as the cheap layer type in a hybrid where full attention every few blocks covers the recall it cannot do.
mechanisms.avoid: As a drop-in replacement for attention in a retrieval-heavy model. Pure linear attention still loses on exact-recall benchmarks, and no amount of tuning has closed that gap; the fix was better update rules, not better feature maps.
mechanisms.shipped: Rarely pure. Its descendants ship everywhere: RWKV, RetNet, Mamba, GLA, Gated DeltaNet, MiniMax-01, Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear
