citation.authors: Angelos Katharopoulos, Apoorv Vyas, Nikolaos Pappas, François Fleuret (Idiap / EPFL / U. Washington)

mechanisms.name: Local + global + random sparse attention (BigBird)
mechanisms.problem: Sparse patterns worked empirically, but nobody could say what was being given up. Is a sparse attention Transformer still a universal approximator? Is it still Turing complete? Or is it a heuristic that happens to work?
how: Combine three patterns: a window for locality, a few global tokens attending everywhere, and a handful of random edges per query.

The random edges are the theoretical contribution. They turn the attention pattern into an expander graph, which mixes in O(log n) hops, and the paper proves the resulting model remains a universal approximator of sequence functions and is Turing complete.
Implemented block-wise rather than token-wise so it maps onto dense GPU matmuls instead of gather operations.
pros: The only sparse method of its era with real theory behind it - it tells you what you keep, not just what you save.
Linear complexity with 8× longer sequences on the same hardware, and strong results on long-document QA and summarisation.
Block-wise implementation means the FLOP saving actually becomes a wall-clock saving.
Random edges are a genuinely good idea: they guarantee mixing without anyone having to guess which long-range connections matter.
cons: The theory is asymptotic and the constants are brutal. Universal approximation "with enough layers" is not a claim about your 24-layer model, and the paper is explicit that sparse attention can need many more layers to match dense.
Random edges are unstructured memory access - a genuinely awkward fit for tensor cores, which is why it needs the block-wise reformulation to be fast at all.
Primarily an encoder story; the causal variant loses much of the benefit.
Like all fixed patterns, the design is a guess made before the model sees data.
mechanisms.pick: Long-document encoder work - QA, summarisation, genomics - where you want linear cost with a theoretical safety net.
mechanisms.avoid: Autoregressive decoding at scale. The 2025 trainable-sparsity methods beat it on both quality and hardware efficiency.
mechanisms.shipped: BigBird, BigBird-Pegasus; the local+global recipe persists widely

citation.title: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
citation.authors: Manzil Zaheer, Guru Guruganesh, Avinava Dubey, Joshua Ainslie, Chris Alberti, Santiago Ontañón, Philip Pham, Anirudh Ravula, Qifan Wang, Li Yang, Amr Ahmed (Google Research)

mechanisms.name: Random-feature softmax approximation (Performer)
mechanisms.problem: Linear attention is fast but it replaces softmax with something that is not softmax, and quality suffers. Could you get the linear-time reassociation trick while still approximating the actual softmax kernel, with an error bound?
how: Use random features to build an unbiased estimator of the softmax kernel: exp(q·k) ≈ φ(q)·φ(k) where φ is a random projection followed by an exponential. Then reassociate exactly as in linear attention.

The FAVOR+ contribution is making those features positive and orthogonal. Earlier trigonometric random features gave negative values and catastrophic variance when the true attention weights were near zero, which is most of them.
Because it approximates softmax rather than replacing it, an existing pretrained Transformer can in principle be converted with only light finetuning.
pros: Approximates the real thing with provable, unbiased error rather than substituting a different similarity function.
Linear time and space, causal masking supported, no sparsity pattern to design.
Can convert a pretrained dense model rather than requiring training from scratch - unique among the 2020 zoo.
cons: Unbiased is not the same as accurate. Variance shrinks only as 1/r, so getting a good approximation needs many features, and by the time you have enough the speed advantage is largely gone.
The error compounds across layers, and the failure mode is worst exactly where attention is sharpest - which is where it matters most.
Empirically it underperforms dense attention on tasks requiring precise retrieval, and the gap did not close with tuning.
Large constant factors mean it only pays off at long sequence lengths.
mechanisms.pick: Long-sequence scientific or non-text workloads where attention is genuinely diffuse - protein sequences, some vision settings - and an unbiased approximation is an acceptable trade.
mechanisms.avoid: Language models that must retrieve exactly. FlashAttention gets you exactness at competitive speed and made the whole approximate-softmax line hard to justify.
mechanisms.shipped: Performer; the random-feature idea persists in some efficient-attention research

citation.title: Rethinking Attention with Performers
citation.authors: Krzysztof Choromanski, Valerii Likhosherstov, David Dohan, Xingyou Song, Andreea Gane, Tamás Sarlós, Peter Hawkins, Jared Davis, Afroz Mohiuddin, Lukasz Kaiser, David Belanger, Lucy Colwell, Adrian Weller (Google / DeepMind / Cambridge)

mechanisms.name: The delta rule (fast weight programmers)
mechanisms.problem: Linear attention's recurrent state is updated by pure addition: St = St-1 + ktvtᵀ. Nothing is ever removed. Write to the same key twice and both values are in there, superimposed. The state saturates, retrieval smears, and quality collapses on long sequences. Adding is not writing.
how: Recognise the linear-attention state as a fast weight matrix: an associative memory being programmed on the fly by the slow weights. Then borrow the classical delta rule from associative-memory literature: before writing a new value at key k, read out what is currently stored there and write only the difference.

St = St-1 + βt kt(vt - St-1kt)ᵀ. This is a rank-one edit - it overwrites the old association instead of piling on top of it. Equivalently, it is one step of online gradient descent on a memory-reconstruction loss.
The result is a fixed-size memory that can be genuinely revised, so capacity is spent on what is still relevant rather than on an accumulating pile of everything ever written.
mechanisms.math: Sₜ = Sₜ₋₁ + βₜ kₜ (vₜ − Sₜ₋₁kₜ)ᵀ
pros: Fixes the single worst defect of linear attention - the state can now be corrected, not just accumulated - and it does so with no increase in state size.
Dramatically better on associative-recall tasks than additive linear attention, which is exactly the axis where linear models lose to Transformers.
Principled: the update is an online learning step, so the memory has a loss it is descending rather than a heuristic it is following.
Reframes the whole family. Once you see the state as a programmable weight matrix, you can ask what the best update rule is, and that question drives the next four years.
cons: The update is sequential and looks unparallelisable - each step depends on reading the previous state. That is why this sat mostly unused for three years, until a chunkwise-parallel formulation (DeltaNet, 2024) made it trainable at scale.
Still a fixed-size state, so it still cannot do exact recall of arbitrary content the way full attention can - it manages a bounded memory better, it does not remove the bound.
There is no forgetting term. It can overwrite a key it is written to again, but it cannot decide to let old, untouched information decay. That gap is what gating later fills.
Numerically more delicate than plain accumulation, and the extra read-modify-write costs wall-clock time per step.
mechanisms.pick: As the update rule inside any linear/recurrent layer you are designing. In 2025 there is little reason to build an additive linear-attention layer when a delta-rule layer costs about the same.
mechanisms.avoid: On its own as a whole architecture. Without gating it forgets nothing by choice, and without interleaved full attention it still cannot retrieve exactly.
mechanisms.shipped: DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and via that route into Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear

citation.title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
citation.authors: Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie, Jürgen Schmidhuber (IDSIA / USI / SUPSI)
citation.note: The delta rule itself is far older - Widrow-Hoff, 1960 - and Schmidhuber's fast-weight work dates to 1992. This paper is dated here because it is where the connection to linear attention is made explicit and the modern DeltaNet line begins. The parallel training algorithm that made it practical came later: Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length, arXiv:2406.06484.

mechanisms.name: Rotary position embedding (RoPE)
mechanisms.problem: Additive position embeddings put position and content into the same vector and hope attention untangles them. Relative schemes fixed the semantics but cost memory and blocked fast kernels. Could position be encoded so that the attention score depends only on relative distance, with no added term at all?
how: Treat each pair of embedding dimensions as a point in a 2D plane and rotate it by an angle proportional to the absolute position: θi = m · base-2i/d. Do this to queries and keys before the dot product; do nothing to values.

Because rotations compose, the inner product of a rotated query at position m and a rotated key at position n depends only on m - n. Absolute rotation in, relative dependence out. No bias term, no extra tensor, no extra memory.

Different dimension pairs rotate at geometrically spaced frequencies, so low dimensions track fine local offsets and high dimensions track coarse document-scale position. Averaged over dimensions you get a natural long-term decay: nearby tokens interact strongly, distant ones weakly.
The base (usually 10000) sets the slowest wavelength. That single scalar turns out to be the handle the entire context-extension family grabs onto.
mechanisms.math: ⟨Rₘq, Rₙk⟩ = ⟨q, Rₙ₋ₘk⟩   —   score depends on (m − n) only
pros: Relative semantics at zero parameter and near-zero memory cost, applied inside the attention computation rather than bolted onto the input.

Composes perfectly with KV caching and with fused kernels like FlashAttention, because it is applied to q and k before the matmul and adds nothing to the score matrix. This is the practical reason it won.
The decay with distance emerges from the construction rather than being imposed - it is a consequence of the frequency spread, not a hand-tuned prior.
The base is a tuning knob you can turn after training. That accidental property is what made cheap context extension possible in 2023 and is arguably worth more than the mechanism itself.
cons: It does not extrapolate. Past the training length the rotation angles reach combinations never seen and attention degenerates - often catastrophically, not gracefully. Every method in the context-extension family exists because of this one sentence.
The highest-frequency dimensions complete many full rotations within the training window, so they alias: two very different distances can produce the same angle.
It only encodes position in the score, so the value vectors carry no positional information - a subtle expressive restriction relative to Shaw-style schemes.
Long-term decay is a prior, and occasionally the wrong one: a genuinely important token 50k back is penalised for being far away.
mechanisms.pick: Essentially every decoder-only LLM being trained today. It is the default for a reason, and if you are unsure what positional scheme to use, this is the answer.
mechanisms.avoid: If you need robust zero-shot length generalisation with no finetuning and no scaling trick, ALiBi degrades more gracefully. And if you are training at 1M context from scratch, consider a hybrid where only some layers carry RoPE at all.
mechanisms.shipped: Llama 1-4, GPT-NeoX, PaLM, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek, Phi, and essentially every open-weight LLM since 2022

citation.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
citation.authors: Jianlin Su, Yu Lu, Shengfeng Pan, Ahmed Murtadha, Bo Wen, Yunfeng Liu (Zhuiyi Technology)
citation.note: Su had described the idea in Chinese-language blog posts on kexue.fm before the arXiv preprint. The arXiv v1 date is used here for consistency with every other row, but the idea circulated slightly earlier - a good example of why "first appearance" needs a stated definition.

mechanisms.name: ALiBi (attention with linear biases)
mechanisms.problem: Training at long context is expensive; inference at long context is desirable. Could you train on 1k tokens and run on 10k without any finetuning at all? Every positional scheme then available said no.
how: Remove positional embeddings entirely. Instead subtract a penalty from each attention score proportional to the distance between query and key: score = q·k + m·(j - i), where m is a fixed negative slope.

Each head gets a different slope, in a geometric sequence (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...). Steep-slope heads are forced to be local; shallow-slope heads can see far. The model gets a range of receptive fields for free.

Because the penalty is a straight line defined for any distance, feeding a distance never seen in training produces a sensible value rather than an undefined one. Extrapolation degrades smoothly instead of falling off a cliff.
mechanisms.math: softmax( qᵢkⱼᵀ + mₕ · (j − i) ),   mₕ = 2^(−8h/H)
pros: Genuine zero-shot length extrapolation - train at 1024, evaluate at 2048 or beyond with no finetuning and no scaling trick. Nothing before it could do that.
Zero parameters, one addition, trivially simple to implement, and it trains faster and uses less memory than sinusoidal embeddings.
The per-head slope schedule is elegant: it hands the model an explicit multi-scale view of the sequence without anyone having to design one.
Numerically robust and completely predictable - there is no regime where it does something surprising.
cons: It hard-wires a recency prior. ALiBi structurally cannot say "the important token is 30,000 back and nothing since matters" - the linear penalty has already buried it. For retrieval and long-horizon agent work this is a real ceiling.
The extrapolation is real but bounded; quality still degrades well before the extreme lengths modern models advertise.
In practice it behaves rather like a soft sliding window, so the effective context can be considerably shorter than the nominal one - a fact that flatters its perplexity numbers.
The slopes are fixed by hand, not learned, and the geometric schedule is a heuristic that happens to work.
The ecosystem went the other way: RoPE plus YaRN dominates, so ALiBi has less tooling, fewer kernels and less community support.
mechanisms.pick: When you must train short and serve longer with no finetuning budget, when you want zero positional parameters, or in a locality-dominated domain where a recency prior is genuinely correct.
mechanisms.avoid: Long-context retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack workloads, or anything where a distant token must win against recent ones. Also avoid it if you want ecosystem support - RoPE has all of it.
mechanisms.shipped: BLOOM, MPT (7B/30B), Falcon (early variants), BaiChuan-13B

citation.title: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation
citation.authors: Ofir Press, Noah A. Smith, Mike Lewis (University of Washington / Facebook AI Research / Allen Institute for AI)

mechanisms.name: NoPE - no positional encoding at all
mechanisms.problem: Everyone "knows" attention is permutation-equivariant and therefore requires a positional signal. But that argument is about a bidirectional encoder. In a causal decoder, token i can see i tokens and token j can see j - the mask itself is a positional signal. So is the encoding necessary at all?
how: Remove positional encodings entirely from a decoder-only Transformer and train normally. The causal mask breaks permutation equivariance on its own: each position has a distinct number of visible predecessors, and the model can and does count them.
Probing shows these models recover position information internally to a surprising degree, and downstream quality is competitive with explicitly-encoded models at the same scale.
Later work found NoPE decoders often generalise to longer sequences better than explicitly-encoded ones on some tasks - there is no encoding to go out of distribution.
pros: Nothing to extrapolate, because nothing was encoded. No base to scale, no table to overrun, no angles that go out of distribution.
The simplest possible design - one fewer component, one fewer hyperparameter, one fewer thing to get wrong.
Genuinely useful as a negative result: it puts a floor under how much of the positional machinery is load-bearing, which recalibrates every claim made by the rest of this family.
Directly motivates the 2025 hybrid designs where only some layers carry positional information.
cons: Only works for causal decoders. Remove the mask and the model is genuinely order-blind - so this is not a general replacement.
The learned positional signal is implicit and unauditable; you cannot inspect it, control it, or scale it after the fact the way you can with RoPE's base.
Reported to converge more slowly and to need more data - the explicit inductive bias was buying real optimisation help even where it was not strictly necessary.
Evidence at frontier scale is thin. Most NoPE results are at modest model sizes, and "competitive at 1B" is not the same as "competitive at 400B".
mechanisms.pick: As one layer type in a hybrid stack - which is what production models actually do - or for research into length generalisation where an explicit encoding is the thing going wrong.
mechanisms.avoid: As the sole scheme in a large decoder trained from scratch. The convergence cost is real, and the industry answer has been "some layers NoPE", not "all layers NoPE".
mechanisms.shipped: Llama 4 (interleaved NoPE/RoPE layers, marketed as iRoPE); a common ingredient in long-context research stacks

citation.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
citation.authors: Adi Haviv, Ori Ram, Ofir Press, Peter Izsak, Omer Levy (Tel Aviv University / Intel Labs / University of Washington)
citation.note: A second, frequently-cited NoPE paper - The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers, arXiv:2305.19466 (31 May 2023) - is the one that showed NoPE generalises better to longer sequences than explicit schemes. The 2022 paper is the first appearance and is dated accordingly.

mechanisms.name: FlashAttention (IO-aware exact attention)
mechanisms.problem: Three years of the efficiency zoo had been attacking FLOPs. But a profiler said attention was not FLOP-bound - it was bound by reading and writing the n×n score matrix to high-bandwidth memory. The field was optimising the wrong resource.
how: Never materialise the score matrix. Tile Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, compute attention block by block, and use the online softmax trick to keep a running maximum and normaliser so each output block can be finalised without ever seeing the whole row at once.
For the backward pass, recompute the needed blocks from Q, K, V rather than storing them - trading extra FLOPs for far less memory traffic, which is a straight win when you are bandwidth-bound.
The result is bit-exact. Same mathematics, same answer, 2-4× faster and with memory linear rather than quadratic in sequence length.
mechanisms.math: same softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V — computed in tiles, never stored
pros: It gives up literally nothing. No approximation, no dropped tokens, no quality trade - the only free lunch on this entire page.
Made long-context dense attention affordable, which is why frontier models kept using dense attention through the era when everyone expected them to go sparse.
Linear activation memory unlocked much larger batches and longer training contexts on the same hardware.
It reframed the whole field: after this, efficiency work had to justify itself against an exact, fast baseline rather than against naive PyTorch.
cons: Still quadratic in compute. It moves the constant, not the exponent - at 1M tokens you are still doomed, just later.

Deeply hardware-specific. Each version is hand-tuned per GPU generation, and FlashAttention-2 and -3 exist because the previous one did not use the newest hardware well. Non-NVIDIA support has consistently lagged.

Fusing everything into one kernel makes the attention block rigid: any mechanism needing a custom bias or an unusual mask needs its own kernel written, which quietly disadvantages research ideas that do not fit the template.
It is not a mechanism at all, so it cannot be reasoned about mathematically - it is an implementation, and it has to be re-earned on every new accelerator.
mechanisms.pick: Always. If you are running attention on an NVIDIA GPU and not using a FlashAttention-class kernel, you are leaving a large multiple on the table for no benefit whatsoever.
mechanisms.avoid: There is no case for avoiding it. The honest caveat is only that it does not remove the quadratic term, so it is not a substitute for a sparse or linear mechanism at extreme length.
mechanisms.shipped: PyTorch SDPA, every major training and serving stack - vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, JAX, Megatron

citation.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
citation.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré (Stanford / SUNY Buffalo)
citation.note: Included even though it is a kernel and not a mechanism, because on a chronological axis it is the single most consequential entry between 2020 and 2023: it is the reason most of the efficiency zoo above it never shipped. Successors: FlashAttention-2 (arXiv:2307.08691, 17 Jul 2023) and FlashAttention-3 (arXiv:2407.08608, 11 Jul 2024).

mechanisms.name: Grouped-query attention (GQA)
mechanisms.problem: MQA cut the KV cache by a factor of the head count but cost real quality and was unstable to train. MHA had the quality but an unaffordable cache. The gap between 1 KV head and 32 KV heads had simply never been explored - and there was no way to get a good MQA model without training one from scratch.
how: Interpolate. Divide the h query heads into g groups and give each group its own key and value head. g = h is MHA; g = 1 is MQA; the interesting answers are in between, and in practice g = 8 is the near-universal choice.

The second contribution matters as much as the first: an uptraining recipe. Mean-pool the existing KV heads within each group and continue training for about 5% of the original compute. You can convert a trained MHA checkpoint rather than starting over.
The quality curve turned out to be sharply non-linear. Nearly all of MQA's saving is available at nearly none of its quality loss - the damage is concentrated at the very last step down to one head.
mechanisms.math: cache = 2 · L · g · d_h per token,  1 ≤ g ≤ H
pros: The dominant point on the quality-memory curve, which is why it went from paper to industry default in about two months. Llama 2 70B shipped it in July 2023.
Uptraining means existing checkpoints can be converted cheaply - a huge practical advantage over MQA.
g is a genuine dial: tune it per deployment against your memory budget rather than accepting an architectural verdict.
More stable to train than MQA, and it composes with sliding windows, MLA-style compression and quantisation.
cons: It is an interpolation, not an idea. It relieves the KV cache by a constant factor; the cache still grows linearly with context, so at 1M tokens you have the same problem 4× later.
There is still a measurable quality gap to full MHA, usually small but real, and it shows up most on tasks needing fine-grained retrieval.
The optimal g is empirical - 8 is folklore that happens to work, not a derived value.
It saves nothing during prefill, where you are compute-bound; it is a decode-phase optimisation only.
mechanisms.pick: Almost every decoder-only LLM being trained today. It is close to a free win, and g=8 is a defensible default you will rarely regret.
mechanisms.avoid: If the KV cache is still your binding constraint after GQA - very long context, very high concurrency - a constant factor is not enough and you want MLA or a hybrid with linear layers.
mechanisms.shipped: Llama 2 70B, Llama 3 (all sizes), Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen 2/3, Gemma 2/3, Phi-3, Command R, and nearly everything else

citation.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
citation._titleNote: verified verbatim against the arXiv abstract page - the widely-copied variant reading 'Multi-Query Transformer Checkpoints' is wrong
citation.authors: Joshua Ainslie, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebrón, Sumit Sanghai (Google Research)
citation.note: Three and a half years after MQA. Nothing in the mathematics changed in the interim - what changed is that the industry started serving models at scale, and bandwidth became the bill that hurt.

mechanisms.name: KV cache eviction by heavy hitters (H2O)
mechanisms.problem: MQA and GQA shrink the cache per token. But the cache still grows with every token generated, forever. The other axis nobody had attacked: could you simply throw some tokens out of the cache?
how: Observe that accumulated attention scores are extremely skewed - a small set of tokens ("heavy hitters") receives the overwhelming majority of attention mass across all queries, and that set is remarkably stable over time.

Keep a running sum of attention received per cached token. When the cache exceeds budget, evict the lowest scorers, keeping heavy hitters plus a recent window. The paper frames this as a dynamic submodular-maximisation problem with a greedy approximation.
Reported up to 5× smaller cache with negligible quality loss at moderate budgets, and large end-to-end throughput gains.
pros: Turns an unbounded cache into a bounded one, which is a qualitative change rather than a constant factor - you can serve arbitrarily long streams in fixed memory.
Works on an already-trained model at inference time; no retraining, no architecture change.
The empirical observation underneath it - that attention mass is extremely concentrated and stable - is one of the most reusable findings of 2023.
Composes with GQA, quantisation and windowing.
cons: Eviction is irreversible. If a token turns out to matter 50,000 steps later, it is not there any more, and the model cannot signal that it needs it back. This is a silent failure - the output is fluent and wrong.
Attention-score-based importance is a proxy, and it is measured on the queries seen so far; it cannot anticipate a future question about a currently-boring token.
Per-head, per-layer bookkeeping adds real overhead and complicates paged-cache implementations.
Benchmarks that reward fluency hide the damage. Needle-in-a-haystack tests expose it immediately.
mechanisms.pick: Long-running streaming or chat sessions with a hard memory ceiling, where recent coherence matters more than exact recall of arbitrary earlier content.
mechanisms.avoid: Retrieval-heavy work, long documents you will be asked precise questions about, or agent traces where an early tool result is needed much later. Consider offloading the full cache instead of evicting from it.
mechanisms.shipped: H2O; the idea is widespread in serving stacks as SnapKV, Scissorhands, PyramidKV and similar

citation.title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
citation.authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Ying Sheng, Tianyi Zhou, Tianlong Chen, Lianmin Zheng, Ruisi Cai, Zhao Song, Yuandong Tian, Christopher Ré, Clark Barrett, Zhangyang Wang, Beidi Chen (UT Austin / Stanford / Meta / CMU)

mechanisms.name: Linear position interpolation (PI)
mechanisms.problem: Llama had a 2048-token context and open weights. Everybody wanted more. Extrapolating RoPE past the training length produced catastrophic garbage - attention scores exploded, perplexity went to thousands. The question was suddenly urgent and extremely practical.
how: Do not extrapolate - interpolate. Divide every position index by a scale factor s before applying RoPE, so a 8192-token sequence is compressed into the 0-2048 range the model was actually trained on. Every angle the model sees is one it has seen before.
The insight is that RoPE fails on extrapolation but is well-behaved on interpolation: positions between trained integers are in-distribution, positions beyond them are not.
A short finetune - the paper reports as little as 1000 steps - repairs the loss of resolution and yields a working 32k model from a 2k one.
mechanisms.math: m → m / s   (s = target length / trained length)
pros: Astonishingly cheap. A 16× context extension for a finetune measured in GPU-hours, on a model somebody else trained. This is what made long context a commodity in the open ecosystem.
One line of code. Divide the position index. No architectural change, no new parameters.
Stable and predictable - unlike extrapolation, it has no cliff.
It established the frame every later method works inside: extension is a question of how you map unseen positions onto seen ones.
cons: It blurs local detail. Squashing all positions uniformly means adjacent tokens now sit at angles that were previously a fraction of a position apart, and the high-frequency dimensions that resolve nearby ordering lose precision. Short-context quality measurably regresses.
Uniform scaling is the wrong prior: dimensions with short wavelengths already fit inside the window and did not need interpolating at all. Fixing that is precisely what NTK-aware scaling and YaRN do.
It requires finetuning. It is not a zero-shot method, whatever the community sometimes implies.
Extension factors much beyond 8-16× degrade badly - the resolution loss compounds.
mechanisms.pick: As a baseline and as a teaching example. If you are extending context today, use YaRN instead - but PI is the idea YaRN is a refinement of, and it is still a perfectly serviceable 2-4× extension.
mechanisms.avoid: Large extension factors, or any case where short-context quality must not regress. Also avoid assuming it works without finetuning.
mechanisms.shipped: Llama 2 long-context variants, Code Llama (with base scaling), countless community finetunes

citation.title: Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation
citation.authors: Shouyuan Chen, Sherman Wong, Liangjian Chen, Yuandong Tian (Meta AI)
citation.note: Discovered independently and near-simultaneously outside academia. kaiokendev published the same linear-interpolation trick alongside the SuperHOT LLaMA finetunes: the companion repository kaiokendev/cutoff-len-is-context-len has a first commit dated 21 June 2023 reading "Add dope for extending context to 8K" - six days before the Meta preprint. The Meta paper carries the citable date; the commit log carries the priority. This is a good illustration of why "first appearance" needs a stated definition, and why this page states one.

mechanisms.name: NTK-aware scaled RoPE
mechanisms.problem: Position interpolation squashes every RoPE frequency by the same factor. But the frequencies are doing different jobs: the fast ones already fit many full rotations inside the training window and encode fine local order, while only the slow ones actually run out of room. Uniform squashing destroys local resolution to fix a problem that only exists at the low frequencies.
how: Do not touch the positions. Change the base instead: base' = base · sd/(d-2). Because RoPE frequencies are base-2i/d, raising the base stretches the slow (high-dimension) wavelengths a lot and the fast (low-dimension) ones hardly at all.

The effect is a non-uniform interpolation: high-frequency dimensions keep their resolution and stay in-distribution, low-frequency dimensions get the reach. You spend the interpolation budget where it is actually needed.
The name comes from a Neural Tangent Kernel argument about networks struggling to learn high-frequency components - hence "do not compress the high frequencies".
Dynamic NTK is the natural refinement: scale the base as a function of the current sequence length, so short prompts get no scaling at all and pay no penalty.
mechanisms.math: base → base · s^(d/(d−2))    (instead of  m → m/s)
pros: Works with no finetuning at all, which PI does not. That single property is why it spread across the open-weight ecosystem within days.
Preserves short-context quality far better than PI, because local resolution is left intact.
It is one number in a config file. rope_theta is now a standard field in essentially every model config precisely because of this.
Dynamic scaling means you pay only for the length you are actually using.
cons: The theoretical justification is loose. The NTK argument is a motivating analogy, not a derivation, and the exponent d/(d-2) is a heuristic that was tuned empirically. It works better than it is explained.
Some intermediate dimensions still end up slightly out of distribution - it improves on PI's uniform mistake without fully solving the problem, which is the gap YaRN closes.
Zero-shot quality still degrades past roughly 4-8×; for larger factors you need finetuning anyway.
Because it changes the base rather than the positions, mixing it with other scaling schemes is confusing and easy to get subtly wrong.
mechanisms.pick: You have a pretrained RoPE model, you need moderately more context right now, and you have no training budget. This is still the fastest useful answer available.
mechanisms.avoid: Extreme extension factors, or production systems where you can afford the short finetune that YaRN wants - YaRN is strictly better there.
mechanisms.shipped: Llama 2 and 3 long-context variants, Code Llama (base 1e6), Qwen, and as `rope_scaling: dynamic` across the Hugging Face ecosystem

citation.title: NTK-Aware Scaled RoPE allows LLaMA models to have extended (8k+) context size without any fine-tuning and minimal perplexity degradation
citation.authors: Reddit user "bloc97", posted to r/LocalLLaMA
citation.note: The weakest date on this page and deliberately flagged as such. This mechanism never had a paper of its own - it was a Reddit post, and it was absorbed into production models within weeks. Best available evidence (an archived mirror of the thread and a GitHub issue that cross-references it) places the post at 29 June 2023, and the post ID 14lz7j5 is consistent with that week. Reddit now requires authentication, so this could not be confirmed by loading the page itself - treat the day as high-confidence but not primary-source. It is included because pretending it was a paper would be a much worse distortion than a possibly-imprecise day.

mechanisms.name: YaRN (yet another RoPE extension)
mechanisms.problem: PI interpolated everything uniformly and lost local resolution. NTK-aware scaling stretched the base and mostly fixed that, but by a heuristic that still leaves some dimensions out of distribution. Nobody had asked the obvious question: which dimensions actually need interpolating?
how: Classify each RoPE dimension by its wavelength relative to the training context. Dimensions whose wavelength is much shorter than the trained window have completed many full rotations and are fine - leave them completely alone. Dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the window have never completed a rotation - interpolate those fully. Ramp smoothly in between. This is NTK-by-parts.

Add a second, unrelated correction: as you extend context, average attention entropy rises and the distribution flattens. YaRN compensates with a temperature factor on the attention logits, t ≈ 0.1·ln(s) + 1, folded into the rotation so it costs nothing at runtime.

The result reaches 128k context with roughly 10× fewer tokens and 2.5× fewer training steps than previous methods, and it transfers - a model extended with YaRN can be extended further without starting over.
mechanisms.math: per-dimension ramp by wavelength + logit temperature t ≈ 0.1·ln(s) + 1
pros: The best quality-per-training-token in the extension family, and the current default. It is what you should actually use.
Principled where its predecessors were heuristic: it asks what each dimension is doing and treats it accordingly, instead of applying one rule to all of them.
The temperature correction addresses a real, separate failure mode (entropy drift) that nobody else had even named.
Composes with sliding windows and with dynamic scaling, and needs no architectural change - just a modified RoPE.
Extension is compounding: 8k → 64k → 128k without retraining from scratch each time.
cons: It still requires finetuning - cheap, but not zero. Pure NTK-aware scaling remains the only truly free option.
More hyperparameters than anything before it (ramp boundaries α and β, temperature scale), and the published values are tuned for Llama-family models. They are not universal.

It extends the positional range but cannot create long-range ability the base model never had. A model finetuned on 400 steps of 128k data has a 128k window and often much less than 128k of genuine reach - the effective context lags the nominal one, and benchmarks routinely conflate the two.
Quality still degrades at the extremes; 128k does not mean 128k of uniform quality, and perplexity hides this.
mechanisms.pick: You have a pretrained RoPE model, you need a lot more context, and you can afford a few hundred finetuning steps. That is the modal situation, and YaRN is the modal answer.
mechanisms.avoid: Zero training budget - use dynamic NTK. And do not use it to claim a context length you have not actually evaluated at; measure effective context, not the config value.
mechanisms.shipped: Qwen 2.5 / 3 (128k via YaRN), Nous-Hermes long-context models, DeepSeek variants, widely available in vLLM and Hugging Face

citation.title: YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models
citation.authors: Bowen Peng, Jeffrey Quesnelle, Honglu Fan, Enrico Shippole (Nous Research / EleutherAI / University of Geneva)
citation.note: Note the authorship: Nous Research and EleutherAI, not a frontier lab. Bowen Peng is "bloc97" - the same person who posted NTK-aware scaling to Reddit two months earlier. The community discovery and the formal paper are literally the same author, roughly nine weeks apart.

mechanisms.name: PagedAttention (virtual memory for the KV cache)
mechanisms.problem: Serving systems allocated one contiguous KV buffer per request, sized for the maximum possible output length. Measured waste was 60-80% of all KV memory - internal fragmentation, external fragmentation, and no way to share anything between requests with a common prefix. The mechanism was fine; the memory allocator was the bottleneck.
how: Apply operating-system virtual memory to the KV cache. Split it into fixed-size blocks (pages) that need not be contiguous, and keep a per-sequence block table mapping logical positions to physical blocks.
Allocate blocks on demand as generation proceeds, so nothing is reserved for output that never happens. Waste drops to under one block per sequence.

Copy-on-write sharing: sequences with a common prefix - a shared system prompt, parallel samples from one prompt, a beam search - point at the same physical blocks until they diverge. In many production workloads this is the single largest saving.
pros: 2-4× throughput on unchanged models - no retraining, no quality loss, no architecture change. Pure systems work.
Prefix sharing is close to free and is enormously valuable in real deployments where thousands of requests share a system prompt.
Makes memory usage predictable, which makes serving capacity plannable instead of a guess with a large safety margin.
Became the industry standard almost immediately; vLLM's design is now assumed by everything around it.
cons: Not a mechanism - it changes nothing about attention and saves nothing about the fundamental cost. A paged cache for a 1M-token context is still a 1M-token context.
The block indirection needs custom attention kernels, which adds a maintenance burden and lags new hardware and new attention variants.
Block size is a real tuning parameter with a genuine trade between fragmentation and kernel efficiency.
Adds meaningful complexity to the serving stack - scheduling, preemption and swapping all become part of your problem.
mechanisms.pick: Any production serving deployment. This is table stakes now, and if you are writing your own server you should be copying it.
mechanisms.avoid: Single-user local inference, where the added complexity buys you very little.
mechanisms.shipped: vLLM, and adopted in TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, TGI and essentially every modern serving stack

citation.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
citation.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica (UC Berkeley / Stanford / UCSD)
citation.note: Included for the same reason as FlashAttention: on a chronological axis, the systems entries explain why several mathematically elegant mechanisms above them never needed to ship.

mechanisms.name: Attention sinks (StreamingLLM)
mechanisms.problem: The obvious way to stream indefinitely is a sliding-window KV cache: evict the oldest token when full. In practice this destroys the model instantly - perplexity explodes the moment the very first tokens are evicted, even though those tokens are semantically meaningless. Nobody could explain why.
how: The diagnosis is the contribution. Softmax forces every attention row to sum to 1. A head that has nothing it wants to attend to must still put its mass somewhere, and models learn to dump it on the first few tokens - which every query can see and which carry little content. These are attention sinks: a learned no-op, a place to park unwanted probability mass.
Evict the sinks and that mass is forcibly redistributed onto real tokens, corrupting every attention distribution in the model at once. Hence the cliff.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: keep the first four tokens permanently, and slide the window over everything else. Four tokens. That restores stable generation over 4 million tokens with no finetuning at all.
The paper also shows that pretraining with a single dedicated sink token gives an even cleaner result - which is why frontier models now ship an explicit learnable sink.
mechanisms.math: cache = { first k tokens }  ∪  { last W tokens },   k ≈ 4
pros: An enormous effect for a four-token change, with no retraining - one of the highest ratios of impact to complexity on this page.
It is a genuine explanation, not a patch. It named a real phenomenon that turned out to matter for quantisation, for outlier features, for interpretability and for KV compression.
Enables truly unbounded streaming in constant memory - millions of tokens without a reset.
Composes with everything: windows, GQA, quantisation, paged caches.
cons: It restores fluency, not memory. This is the most misread result in long-context work. The model streams stably over 4M tokens; it cannot recall anything from outside its window. Coherence is not context.
The effective context remains the window size - so this is a fix for a sliding window's failure mode, not a long-context mechanism.
The sink is a symptom of softmax's forced normalisation. Preserving it treats the symptom; alternatives such as an explicit off-value in the denominator address the cause but need retraining.
The magic number four is empirical, and it varies somewhat by model and by training recipe.
mechanisms.pick: Any streaming or always-on deployment with a bounded cache - long-running chat, live transcription, monitoring. If you are evicting from a KV cache at all, you need this.
mechanisms.avoid: As a way to get long context. It does not give you any. Pair it with retrieval or a hybrid architecture if the model must actually remember.
mechanisms.shipped: Hugging Face `sink_cache`, vLLM, llama.cpp; explicit learnable sinks ship in Mistral, Gemma 2/3 and OpenAI's GPT-OSS

citation.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
citation.authors: Guangxuan Xiao, Yuandong Tian, Beidi Chen, Song Han, Mike Lewis (MIT / Meta AI / CMU)

mechanisms.name: Ring attention (blockwise, device-parallel)
mechanisms.problem: FlashAttention removed the quadratic memory cost on one device. But a single device still has to hold the whole sequence's activations, so context length was capped by one GPU's memory no matter how many GPUs you owned.
how: Shard the sequence across devices. Each device holds a block of queries permanently and passes its block of keys and values around a ring of devices, accumulating partial attention outputs with the same online-softmax trick FlashAttention uses.
Because the KV communication is overlapped with the block-local attention computation, the communication is effectively free when block sizes are chosen well.
Context length now scales with the number of devices, with no approximation at all. Million-token contexts become an engineering problem rather than an architectural one.
pros: Exact - like FlashAttention it approximates nothing, it just distributes the computation.
Context scales linearly with device count, which is the only mechanism here that makes 1M+ context possible without giving anything up.
Composes with every other mechanism, since it changes only where the computation happens.
It is the reason very-long-context frontier models became feasible at all in 2024.
cons: Total compute is still quadratic - you are buying memory headroom with hardware, not reducing work. The bill gets paid, just by more machines.
Needs many devices and fast interconnect; it is useless if you have one GPU, which is most people.
Load balancing under a causal mask is genuinely awkward - the device holding the last block does far more work than the first - and needs careful striping to fix.
Implementation complexity is high and it interacts subtly with every other form of parallelism in your stack.
mechanisms.pick: Training or prefilling very long contexts on a cluster you already have. If your context does not fit on one device and you refuse to approximate, this is the answer.
mechanisms.avoid: Single-device work, and decode-heavy serving - it addresses prefill and training, not the per-token bandwidth cost of generation.
mechanisms.shipped: Context/sequence parallelism in Megatron-LM, JAX and DeepSpeed; widely believed to underpin the 1M-token frontier models

citation.title: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
citation.authors: Hao Liu, Matei Zaharia, Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley)

mechanisms.name: Selective state space (Mamba)
mechanisms.problem: State space models were linear-time and elegant but their dynamics were fixed - the same recurrence applied to every token regardless of content. That made them fast and fundamentally unable to do content-based reasoning: they could not decide to remember this token and forget that one.
how: Make the state-space parameters functions of the input. The step size, the input matrix and the output matrix are all computed from the current token, so the recurrence can decide, per token, how much to write and how much to forget.

That breaks the convolutional formulation that made SSMs fast, so the paper contributes a hardware-aware parallel scan that keeps the state in SRAM and never materialises it in HBM - the same IO-aware philosophy as FlashAttention, applied to a recurrence.

Result: linear scaling in sequence length, constant memory during generation, 5× higher inference throughput than a Transformer of matching size, and quality competitive with Transformers twice its size at the scales tested.
mechanisms.math: hₜ = Ā(xₜ) hₜ₋₁ + B̄(xₜ) xₜ   —   parameters depend on the input
pros: Restores selectivity to a recurrent model - the missing ingredient that had kept SSMs from competing with attention on language.
Linear time, constant-memory generation, no KV cache at all. At 100k+ tokens this is a categorical advantage rather than a constant factor.
The gating is the key idea the rest of the field adopted: it is what lets a fixed state decide what to forget, which the delta rule alone could not do.
It made "attention is not the only option" a mainstream position again, and forced the field to be explicit about what attention was actually buying.
cons: Exact recall from a fixed-size state is impossible in principle. Mamba underperforms on copying, in-context retrieval and needle-in-a-haystack - and this is a bound, not a bug to be tuned away.
Needs custom CUDA kernels; the parallel scan is not something you express in a few lines of framework code.
The selectivity gains do not obviously persist at frontier scale, and pure Mamba models have not displaced Transformers at the top end.
Much less mature tooling, quantisation support and interpretability than attention - years of ecosystem work would need repeating.
mechanisms.pick: Very long sequences with streaming or bounded-memory requirements, non-language modalities like audio and genomics where exact recall is less critical, or as the cheap layer in a hybrid.
mechanisms.avoid: As a pure replacement in retrieval-heavy language work. Note that the field's own answer was hybrids: Jamba, Zamba and Samba all keep full attention layers, and so do the 2025 production linear models.
mechanisms.shipped: Mamba, Mamba-2, Jamba, Zamba, Codestral Mamba, Falcon Mamba

citation.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
citation.authors: Albert Gu, Tri Dao (CMU / Princeton)
citation.note: Included because on a chronological axis you cannot explain Gated DeltaNet without it: gating is Mamba's contribution and the delta rule is DeltaNet's, and the 2024-2025 mechanisms are explicitly the fusion of the two.

mechanisms.name: Infini-attention (compressive memory in the attention block)
mechanisms.problem: Sliding windows are cheap but forget everything outside the window. Full attention remembers everything but cannot afford to. Could a single attention layer do both - keep exact local attention and hold a bounded, compressed summary of everything older?
how: Inside each attention layer, keep the standard local attention over the current segment, and add a fixed-size associative memory matrix updated with a linear-attention-style rule (optionally the delta rule) from segments as they scroll out of the window.

Query that memory with the same queries used for local attention, and blend the two retrievals with a learned per-head gate. The head decides, per token, how much to trust exact local context versus compressed long-term memory.

Because the old KV entries are folded into a fixed matrix rather than discarded, memory is bounded but nothing is dropped outright - reported at a 114× compression ratio, with 1B models solving passkey retrieval at 1M tokens.
mechanisms.math: output = σ(g)·A_local + (1−σ(g))·A_memory,  memory = fixed d×d state
pros: Bounded memory with unbounded context, and unlike cache eviction nothing is thrown away - it is folded in.
The learned gate is the right design: the model decides when compressed memory is good enough, rather than a human deciding in advance.
Drop-in for a standard attention layer, and it can continue-train from an existing checkpoint rather than needing a fresh pretrain.
It is the clearest single statement of the hybrid thesis - exact recent memory plus compressed distant memory - two years before that became the default design.
cons: The compressed memory is still a fixed-size state, so it has the same hard information bound as linear attention. 114× compression is 114× of lost detail.
Reproduction has been difficult and the results have not been widely replicated at scale, which is a real mark against it.
Passkey retrieval is an easy long-context test - a single distinctive needle. Performance on genuinely diffuse long-context reasoning is much less established.
Adds a second retrieval path and a gate to every layer, which complicates kernels, KV management and interpretability alike.
mechanisms.pick: When you need very long or unbounded context in fixed memory and can tolerate lossy recall of distant material - streaming analysis, long-running assistants.
mechanisms.avoid: Where exact long-range recall is the product. Also be cautious given the thin replication record; a hybrid with real full-attention layers is a better-evidenced choice.
mechanisms.shipped: Not widely deployed; influential as a design pattern rather than as a shipped mechanism

citation.title: Leave No Context Behind: Efficient Infinite Context Transformers with Infini-attention
citation.authors: Tsendsuren Munkhdalai, Manaal Faruqui, Siddharth Gopal (Google)

mechanisms.name: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
mechanisms.problem: GQA and MQA shrink the KV cache by sharing heads, and sharing costs quality because heads can no longer specialise in what they retrieve. Is sharing the only way to make the cache smaller? Or could you keep every head distinct and compress what you store instead?
how: Project the keys and values down into a single low-rank latent vector per token (about 512 dimensions, versus 128 × 128 for full MHA) and cache only that. At attention time, project back up to per-head keys and values.

Crucially, the up-projection matrices can be absorbed into the query and output projections at inference, so the decompression costs no extra matrix multiply in the hot loop. You get the small cache without paying to unpack it.

RoPE breaks this - a rotation applied after compression does not commute with the up-projection - so MLA carries a small set of decoupled RoPE dimensions (64 per token) cached separately and un-compressed. That inelegant-looking detail is what makes the whole thing work.

Net result in DeepSeek-V2: a KV cache 93.3% smaller than MHA, with quality reported as better than MHA rather than merely close - because the low-rank projection acts as a useful regulariser rather than as a lossy shortcut.
mechanisms.math: cache cₜ = W_DKV·hₜ  (≈512 dims) + k_rope (64 dims)   —  per token, per layer
pros: The first KV mechanism that does not trade quality for memory - it compresses rather than shares, and DeepSeek reports it matching or beating full MHA.
Far larger saving than GQA: roughly 4× smaller cache again on top of what GQA already gives you.
The up-projections fold into neighbouring matrices, so the decompression is free at inference.
Proven at frontier scale in production models serving enormous volumes, not just on a benchmark.
cons: Substantially more complex than GQA. The decoupled-RoPE workaround is genuinely fiddly, and a subtly wrong implementation degrades quietly rather than failing loudly.
It must be trained in from the start - there is no cheap uptraining recipe of the kind that made GQA so easy to adopt.
It increases compute during prefill (the up-projections are real work) in exchange for the decode-phase saving, so the win depends on your prompt-to-generation ratio.
Kernel and framework support lagged for a long time, and it is still less universally supported than GQA.
The cache still grows linearly with context - a much better constant, but the same asymptotics.
mechanisms.pick: You are training a large model from scratch and expect to serve it at high concurrency or long context. If the KV cache is your binding constraint and you control pretraining, this is the strongest answer available.
mechanisms.avoid: Adapting an existing checkpoint - use GQA. Also avoid it if your team cannot own a non-trivial attention implementation; complexity is a real cost.
mechanisms.shipped: DeepSeek-V2, V3, R1, V3.2; Kimi K2 and several other frontier Chinese models

citation.title: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
citation.authors: DeepSeek-AI
citation.note: MLA is introduced in §2.1 of the DeepSeek-V2 report, alongside DeepSeekMoE. There is no standalone MLA paper, so the model report is the primary source and the date is its v1.

mechanisms.name: Structured state space duality (Mamba-2)
mechanisms.problem: By 2024 there were two parallel literatures - state space models and linear attention - that behaved similarly, borrowed from each other, and had entirely separate theory and separate kernels. Were they actually the same thing? And if so, could the SSM side stop hand-writing scans and just use a matmul?
how: Prove the duality. A structured state space model with a scalar-times-identity state transition is exactly equivalent to a masked attention computation with a particular semiseparable mask. SSMs and linear attention are two views of one object.

Exploit it: compute the recurrence in a chunkwise form - quadratic attention within a chunk, linear recurrence across chunks. Both halves are dense matrix multiplications, so it runs on tensor cores rather than on a bespoke scan kernel.
Mamba-2 is 2-8× faster to train than Mamba while allowing much larger state sizes, and the chunkwise algorithm becomes the standard training recipe for every linear-memory model after it.
mechanisms.math: SSM(A,B,C) ≡ (L ∘ CBᵀ) x   for semiseparable L   —   chunkwise: quadratic in-chunk, linear cross-chunk
pros: A unification, not just an optimisation - it lets results, kernels and intuitions transfer between two previously separate fields.
The chunkwise-parallel form is the enabling engineering result for the entire 2024-2025 linear-memory wave; Gated DeltaNet and its relatives are all trained this way.
Much larger recurrent states become affordable, which directly improves the recall weakness of linear models.
Runs on standard tensor-core matmuls instead of custom scans, so it is far more portable.
cons: The duality holds for a restricted class of SSMs - scalar state transitions. The most general SSMs are not covered, so some expressiveness is traded for the speedup.
It does nothing about the fundamental limitation: a fixed-size state still cannot do exact recall.
Chunk size becomes another hyperparameter trading parallelism against memory.
It is a training-efficiency result more than a capability result - it makes the family practical, it does not make it better at language.
mechanisms.pick: As the implementation strategy for any linear or recurrent layer you build. In 2025 there is essentially no reason to train one any other way.
mechanisms.avoid: Do not read it as closing the gap with attention on recall - it closes a gap in training throughput.
mechanisms.shipped: Mamba-2, and the chunkwise training algorithm underpins Gated DeltaNet, GLA, RWKV-7, Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear

citation.title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
citation.authors: Tri Dao, Albert Gu (Princeton / CMU)

mechanisms.name: Selective attention (learned context dropping)
mechanisms.problem: Some tokens genuinely stop being useful once they have been read - a disambiguated pronoun, a corrected typo, a finished sub-clause. Standard attention keeps paying for them forever, and every existing eviction scheme decides what to drop with an external heuristic rather than asking the model.
how: Let tokens mask each other. Derive from the existing attention scores an accumulated, causally-masked measure of how much each token has been marked as no-longer-needed by later tokens, and subtract it from future attention logits.
It adds no new parameters - the signal is read out of the attention computation that is already happening.

Once a token's mask is saturated it can be dropped from the KV cache entirely, giving reported memory reductions of 16-47× at equal perplexity, with quality equivalent to a standard Transformer with roughly 2× more heads and parameters.
pros: The model decides what to forget, which is the recurring lesson of this whole timeline - learned selection beats designed selection.
Parameter-free, so the improvement is not just extra capacity in disguise.
Delivers both a quality gain and a large memory saving, which is unusual - most mechanisms here trade one for the other.
Composes naturally with paged caches, since dropped tokens simply free their blocks.
cons: Requires training with it - it is not a post-hoc inference trick you can apply to an existing checkpoint.
Dropping is still irreversible, so a token the model was wrong to discard is unrecoverable.
Evidence base is much thinner than for GQA/MLA - promising results, limited independent replication, no frontier deployment.
The saving is data-dependent, so the memory budget is no longer something you can size in advance.
mechanisms.pick: Research and new pretrains where a smaller cache and better quality are both wanted and you control training. It is the cleanest realisation of "let the model prune its own context".
mechanisms.avoid: Production systems needing a predictable memory ceiling, or anything where you cannot retrain.
mechanisms.shipped: Not yet in a major production model

citation.title: Selective Attention Improves Transformer
citation.authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias (Google Research)
citation.note: Presented at ICLR 2025 but the arXiv v1 is 3 Oct 2024, and this page consistently uses first public appearance - so it sits in 2024, not 2025.

mechanisms.name: Differential attention
mechanisms.problem: A different complaint from everything else on this page - not cost, but accuracy. Softmax attention allocates non-trivial probability mass to irrelevant context, because every row must sum to 1 whether or not anything deserves it. In long contexts that noise floor swamps the signal, and it is a leading suspect for hallucination and for the lost-in-the-middle effect.
how: Borrow differential amplifiers from electrical engineering. Compute two separate softmax attention maps from two query/key pairs, and take their difference: (softmax(Q₁K₁) - λ·softmax(Q₂K₂))V, with λ learned.
Common-mode noise appears in both maps and cancels; genuine signal does not. The resulting attention distribution is much sparser and much more concentrated on relevant tokens.

Reported to need only about 65% of the parameters or training tokens to match a standard Transformer, with large gains on long-context retrieval, in-context learning, and reduced hallucination - plus fewer activation outliers, which helps quantisation.
mechanisms.math: DiffAttn = ( softmax(Q₁K₁ᵀ/√d) − λ·softmax(Q₂K₂ᵀ/√d) ) V
pros: Attacks quality rather than cost, which makes it genuinely different from almost everything else here and a useful reminder that attention's problems are not all about the bill.
Substantially better long-context retrieval and reduced lost-in-the-middle behaviour, which is exactly where long-context models actually disappoint.
Fewer activation outliers means friendlier quantisation - a real, unglamorous deployment benefit.
The mechanism is simple, well-motivated by analogy, and drops into an existing architecture.
cons: Roughly twice the attention computation for the same context - you are buying accuracy with FLOPs, which is the opposite direction to the rest of this page.
λ needs a careful initialisation schedule; the paper's recipe is somewhat delicate and the mechanism is sensitive to it.
Independent replication at frontier scale is limited, and no major production model has adopted it.
It reduces the noise floor; it does not remove the quadratic cost or the KV cache, so it stacks on top of your existing problems rather than solving any of them.
mechanisms.pick: Long-context retrieval and reasoning workloads where correctness matters more than throughput, and you have compute to spend on quality.
mechanisms.avoid: Any deployment that is already compute- or latency-constrained. Doubling attention work to reduce noise is only rational if the noise is what is hurting you.
mechanisms.shipped: Not in a major production model; influential in research

citation.authors: Tianzhu Ye, Li Dong, Yuqing Xia, Yutao Sun, Yi Zhu, Gao Huang, Furu Wei (Microsoft Research)

mechanisms.name: Gated DeltaNet
mechanisms.problem: By late 2024 there were two good ideas for managing a fixed-size recurrent memory and they were in different papers. Mamba's gating lets a state decide what to forget, but its writes are still coarse. The delta rule writes precisely, but has no way to let stale information decay. Each fixes the other's blind spot, and nobody had combined them.
how: Use both update terms at once: St = αt(I - βtktktᵀ)St-1 + βtktvtᵀ. The α term is Mamba-style gated decay - erase broadly when the context shifts. The β projection term is the delta rule - overwrite one specific key precisely.

The two mechanisms are complementary in a concrete way: gating handles when the topic changes and everything should fade; the delta rule handles when one particular fact is superseded. A memory needs both.

Contribute a chunkwise-parallel algorithm (in the Mamba-2 tradition) so the combined rule is actually trainable at scale, and demonstrate it beating Mamba2 and DeltaNet on language modelling, associative recall, in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.
The paper's own headline architectures are hybrids - Gated DeltaNet layers interleaved with sliding-window attention or Mamba2 layers - which is itself the finding.
mechanisms.math: Sₜ = αₜ(I − βₜ kₜkₜᵀ) Sₜ₋₁ + βₜ kₜ vₜᵀ

costs.decode: O(1) per token, no KV cache

pros: The best-performing fixed-state memory rule published, and it beats both parents on exactly the recall tasks where linear models historically lost.
Constant memory generation with no KV cache at all - at 1M tokens this is a categorical advantage over any attention variant.
Genuinely principled: two distinct failure modes of a bounded memory, two distinct terms, each doing a job you can name.
Trainable at scale thanks to the chunkwise algorithm, and now shipping in production models rather than sitting in a paper.
cons: It is still a fixed-size state, so exact recall of arbitrary content remains impossible. Better management of a bounded memory is not an unbounded memory, and no update rule will change that.
The paper's own best results are hybrids with attention layers - which is an honest admission that the mechanism does not stand alone.
Two gates per step means more hyperparameters, trickier initialisation and more ways to be subtly unstable than plain gated linear attention.
Needs specialised kernels; the ecosystem, tooling and interpretability story are years behind attention.
Evaluation is mostly at moderate scale - the frontier has not yet run a pure-GDN model at the top end, and hybrid results confound the attribution.
mechanisms.pick: Long-context or streaming workloads where constant-memory decoding is worth real money, deployed as the majority layer type in a hybrid with periodic full attention. That combination is currently the best cost-quality point available for very long context.
mechanisms.avoid: As a pure architecture for retrieval-heavy work. Note that even its authors do not recommend that.
mechanisms.shipped: Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear (as KDA, a variant), NVIDIA Nemotron hybrids

citation.note: This is the closing of the loop the timeline is built to show: 2020 linear attention re-derives a recurrent state, 2021 the delta rule makes it editable, 2023 Mamba makes it gateable, 2024 this paper fuses them, 2025 it ships.

mechanisms.name: Lightning attention at frontier scale (MiniMax-01)
mechanisms.problem: Linear attention had a five-year record of working beautifully at 100M parameters and never being tried at the top end. The open question was not whether the mathematics worked - it was whether anyone would bet a frontier training run on it.
how: Take an IO-aware, tiled linear attention (the FlashAttention treatment applied to a linear kernel, splitting intra-block and inter-block computation) and scale it to a 456B-parameter MoE model with 45.9B active parameters.
Do not use it everywhere: every eighth layer keeps full softmax attention. Seven cheap layers, one exact layer, repeated.
The result trains at 1M-token context and extrapolates to 4M at inference, with quality competitive with contemporary frontier models.
pros: The existence proof. It showed linear attention is viable at frontier scale, which five years of small-scale papers had not established.
Enormous context at a fraction of the attention cost, with weights released openly so the claim is checkable.
The 7:1 hybrid ratio became a widely-copied reference point for how much exact attention you actually need.
IO-aware implementation means the theoretical linear saving shows up as real wall-clock time.
cons: It is a hybrid, so the linear layers are not carrying the model alone - the full-attention layers are doing the exact retrieval, and the architecture is an admission that pure linear attention is not enough.
The 7:1 ratio is empirical, not derived, and there is no theory saying it transfers to other scales or tasks.
Long-context evaluation at 4M tokens is genuinely hard to do well, and the benchmarks available are weaker than the claim.
A very large MoE is expensive to serve regardless of how cheap its attention is - the attention saving is not the whole system cost.
mechanisms.pick: As evidence when arguing about architecture, and as a template if you are designing a long-context model - the hybrid ratio is the transferable lesson, not the specific kernel.
mechanisms.avoid: Do not read it as "linear attention replaced softmax". One layer in eight is still softmax, deliberately.
mechanisms.shipped: MiniMax-01 (MiniMax-Text-01, MiniMax-VL-01)

mechanisms.name: Native sparse attention (NSA)
mechanisms.problem: Six years of sparse attention had produced almost nothing in production, for two reasons stated bluntly in this paper. First, the patterns were applied post-hoc to models trained densely, so the model never learned to work with them. Second, the theoretical FLOP savings did not survive contact with GPUs - the memory access patterns were wrong.
how: Three branches, computed in parallel for every query and combined by a learned gate: compressed coarse-grained block summaries of the entire history; selected fine-grained blocks chosen by importance scores derived from the compressed branch; and a sliding window for recent local context.

Natively trainable - the selection is differentiable end-to-end and the model is pretrained with sparsity present, so it learns to route information through the pattern rather than having the pattern imposed on a dense model afterwards.

Hardware-aligned - selection operates on blocks sized to GPU memory transactions, with a group-centric data loading scheme designed around GQA and tensor cores. The paper reports up to 9× forward and 6× backward speedups at 64k context, and 11.6× faster decoding.

The headline result is the one nobody expected: the sparse model matches or exceeds full attention on general benchmarks, long-context tasks and chain-of-thought reasoning. Sparsity stopped being a compromise.
mechanisms.math: o = g_cmp·Attn(compressed) + g_slc·Attn(selected) + g_win·Attn(window)
pros: The first sparse attention that is not a compromise - equal or better quality than dense, plus large real speedups. Six years of the sparse literature had never managed both at once.
The three-branch design is genuinely well-reasoned: coarse for everything, fine for what matters, exact for what is near. Each branch covers the others' blind spot.
Hardware-aligned by construction, so the FLOP saving becomes wall-clock saving instead of evaporating.
End-to-end trainable selection means the model owns the decision - the lesson this timeline keeps repeating.
cons: You must pretrain with it. That is the entire point, and it is also a very high barrier - you cannot retrofit it onto an existing model, so only labs training from scratch can use it.
Considerably more complex than dense attention: three branches, a gate, a custom Triton kernel, and a block-selection scheme to keep correct.
The gains are largest at long context; at short context the overhead can make it slower than dense attention with FlashAttention.
It is co-designed with GQA and with specific GPU characteristics, so it inherits assumptions about hardware that may not hold on the next generation.
The 'matches dense' result is from one lab at one scale on their own training recipe; independent replication at other scales is still limited.
mechanisms.pick: You are pretraining a long-context model from scratch and can own a custom kernel. This is the state of the art for making long context affordable without giving up quality.
mechanisms.avoid: Adapting an existing dense checkpoint, short-context workloads, or teams without kernel-engineering capacity.
mechanisms.shipped: The design line leads directly to DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2-Exp

citation.authors: Jingyang Yuan, Huazuo Gao, Damai Dai, Junyu Luo, Liang Zhao, Zhengyan Zhang et al. (DeepSeek-AI / Peking University / University of Washington)

mechanisms.name: Mixture of block attention (MoBA)
mechanisms.problem: The same problem NSA attacked - trainable sparsity - approached from a completely different tradition. Mixture-of-Experts had already solved "let a learned gate pick a sparse subset of things to compute" for feed-forward layers. Why had nobody applied the same routing idea to attention?
how: Partition the sequence into blocks and treat each block as an expert. For each query, a gating network scores blocks by comparing the query to a mean-pooled representation of each block, and routes the query to its top-k blocks (plus its own current block, always).
Attention is then computed only over the selected blocks. The gate is trained end-to-end with the model, so block selection is learned rather than designed.

The property that makes it unusually practical: MoBA and full attention can be switched at will on the same weights. You can train dense and serve sparse, or run dense prefill and sparse decode, or transition gradually during training. No other mechanism here offers that.
Deployed in Kimi's production long-context stack, with reported 6.5× speedup at 1M tokens and 16× at 10M.
mechanisms.math: gate(q, block) = q · mean-pool(K_block);  attend over top-k blocks ∪ {current block}
pros: Seamless switching between sparse and full attention on identical weights - a deployment property worth more in practice than a few percent of throughput.
Conceptually the simplest of the trainable-sparse family: it is MoE routing, a mechanism the field already understands deeply.
Proven in production at Kimi rather than only on benchmarks.
Much less parameter-free hand-design than NSA - one gate, one k, one block size.
cons: Block-granular selection is coarse. A single critical token inside an unselected block is invisible, and mean-pooling a block into one vector is a lossy way to decide whether it matters.
The gate scores against a pooled summary, so a block containing one highly relevant token among many irrelevant ones will score low - exactly the needle-in-a-haystack case.
Top-k routing has the same load-balancing pathologies as MoE, including the risk that some blocks are never selected.
Fewer architectural safeguards than NSA - there is no compressed branch guaranteeing that something is seen from every part of the history.
mechanisms.pick: Long-context serving where you want trainable sparsity but need the option to fall back to full attention - and where a familiar MoE-style mechanism is easier for your team to reason about than a three-branch design.
mechanisms.avoid: Fine-grained retrieval where the needle can hide inside a boring block. NSA's compressed branch is a more robust answer there.
mechanisms.shipped: Kimi (Moonshot AI) production long-context models

citation.title: MoBA: Mixture of Block Attention for Long-Context LLMs
citation.authors: Enzhe Lu, Zhejun Jiang, Jingyuan Liu et al. (Moonshot AI)
citation.note: Two days after NSA, from a different lab, in a different research tradition, reaching the same conclusion: sparsity has to be learned end-to-end. Simultaneous independent arrival is usually a sign the field has found the right question.

mechanisms.name: Multi-token attention
mechanisms.problem: A structural limitation nobody had named: attention weights are decided by the similarity of one query vector to one key vector. If you need to find the place where two particular things co-occur - "Alice" and "rabbit" in the same sentence - a single query vector has to encode both at once, and one vector is a narrow channel for a conjunction.
how: Apply convolutions over the attention logits - across nearby query positions, across nearby key positions, and across heads - before the softmax. An attention weight can then be conditioned on several neighbouring query and key vectors rather than on one pair.
Head-mixing convolution lets one head's evidence sharpen another's, so heads can pool information rather than each voting independently.
Reported gains on language modelling and, most clearly, on long-context tasks that require finding conjunctions of information - which is exactly what the mechanism was designed for.
pros: Identifies a real expressive bottleneck rather than another cost, and the fix follows directly from the diagnosis.
Cheap - small convolutions over logits, not another full attention map.
Targets conjunctive retrieval, which is precisely where long-context models fail in practice and where benchmarks are getting harder.
Composes with existing architectures without changing the overall block structure.
cons: It operates on the attention logit matrix, which FlashAttention specifically never materialises. That is a serious practical problem: the mechanism fights the single most important optimisation in the stack.
Adds kernel-sized hyperparameters with no principled way to choose them.
Very new, single-lab, with no independent replication or production deployment.
The benefit is concentrated on a specific class of task; on general workloads the gains are modest relative to the implementation friction.
mechanisms.pick: Research settings and retrieval-heavy tasks where conjunctive lookups matter and you can afford non-fused attention.
mechanisms.avoid: Anything that depends on FlashAttention-class kernels for throughput, which is most production systems.
mechanisms.shipped: Not deployed; research contribution
